# Transmission, outbreaks and One Health

> *A pathogen persists only if it reaches a new host or survives in a reservoir between hosts. Where
> do microbes live between hosts, how do they travel, and where can transmission be interrupted?*

## The chain of infection {#sec-trans-chain}

Transmission is usually described as a chain of six links. Each link is a point at which the chain
can be broken, so the model is most useful as a checklist for control.

| Link | What it means | Example of breaking it |
|---|---|---|
| Infectious agent | The organism itself | Antimicrobial treatment; sterilisation |
| Reservoir | Where the organism normally lives and multiplies: people, animals, soil or water | Treating infected people; controlling infection in animals; cleaning contaminated water systems |
| Portal of exit | How it leaves the reservoir: respiratory particles, faeces, blood, skin | Covering coughs; dressing wounds |
| Mode of transmission | How it travels (see below) | Hand hygiene; safe water; mosquito control |
| Portal of entry | How it enters the next host: mouth, airway, broken skin, mucosa | Gloves; safe injection practice |
| Susceptible host | A person who can be infected | Vaccination |

An organism whose only reservoir is humans can in principle be eradicated: smallpox was, and polio is
close. An organism with an animal or environmental reservoir cannot be, because it persists whatever
happens in the human population.

A **zoonosis** is an infection transmitted from animals to humans. Around 60% of known human pathogen
species, and about 75% of emerging ones, are zoonotic [@taylor2001risk]. A **vector** is an arthropod
that carries an organism between hosts, usually a mosquito, tick, flea or louse. A **fomite** is an
inanimate object that carries organisms, such as a door handle or a shared keyboard.

## Routes of transmission {#sec-trans-routes}

<div data-island="sorter" data-src="/diagrams/transmission-sorter.yml"></div>

The description of the respiratory route changed during the COVID-19 pandemic. Exhaled particles span
a continuous range of sizes. The older teaching split them into **droplet** transmission, by particles
larger than about 5 µm that fall within a metre or two, and **airborne** transmission, by smaller
particles that stay suspended and can accumulate in poorly ventilated rooms. That fixed cut-off is now
recognised as too rigid [@wang2021airborne]. Control therefore combines distance with ventilation and
shorter exposure.

## Measuring how an infection spreads {#sec-trans-measures}

| Quantity | Question it answers | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Incubation period | How long between infection and symptoms? | Sets how long contacts are observed |
| Infectious period | When can this person pass it on? | May begin before symptoms, which makes control much harder |
| Basic reproduction number, R₀ | How many people does one case infect in a fully susceptible population? | A property of the organism *and* of the population |
| Effective reproduction number, R | How many does one case infect now, given immunity and control measures? | Above 1, cases grow; below 1, the outbreak shrinks |

Because R falls as immunity rises, there is a level of immunity above which an outbreak cannot sustain
itself. This **herd immunity threshold** is 1 − 1/R₀. For an organism with an R₀ of 2 it is 50%; for
a highly transmissible one with an R₀ of 12 it is above 90%, which is why measles needs such high
vaccination coverage.

<div data-island="epidemic-sim" data-src="/diagrams/epidemic-sim.yml"></div>

In the model, the outbreak ends while susceptible people remain, because R falls below 1 before
everyone has been infected. Reducing transmission both lowers the peak and delays it, which is the
reasoning behind measures intended to keep demand within hospital capacity. When R₀ is close to 1, a
small change in it makes a large difference to the final number infected.

## Investigating an outbreak {#sec-trans-outbreak}

An **outbreak** is more cases of a disease than expected in a given place and time. **Endemic** means
constantly present in a population; an **epidemic** is a sharp rise above that baseline; a **pandemic**
is an epidemic across many countries.

Investigation follows a standard sequence:

1. Confirm that the cases are real, and define what counts as a case.
2. Describe the cases by person, place and time.
3. Use that description to form a hypothesis about the source.
4. Test the hypothesis by comparing exposures between people who became ill and people who did not.
5. Act to interrupt transmission, without waiting for the investigation to be complete.

An **epidemic curve**, a plot of cases against time of onset, indicates the type of source. Cases that
cluster within one incubation period suggest a **point-source** outbreak from a single shared
exposure; the wedding lunch case in [*Gram-positive cocci*](../microbes/gram-positive-cocci.qmd#sec-gpc-case)
is an example. Cases spread over successive incubation periods, each wave larger than the last,
suggest a **propagated** outbreak, spread from person to person.

## Hand hygiene: the evidence came first {#sec-trans-semmelweis}

In the Vienna General Hospital in the 1840s, two maternity clinics had very different death rates from
**puerperal fever**, infection after childbirth. Mortality was several times higher in the clinic
staffed by medical students, who came to deliveries from the autopsy room, than in the midwives'
clinic. Ignaz Semmelweis reasoned that something was being carried on hands from the dead to the
living, and from May 1847 required staff to wash their hands in chlorinated lime. Mortality in his
clinic fell from 11.4% in 1846 to about 1.3% in 1848 [@semmelweis1861].

Germ theory was still decades away, so Semmelweis could not say what was being carried, and his
colleagues largely rejected the finding. He acted on a route he could interrupt without knowing the
agent, as John Snow did in the case at the end of this chapter. WHO guidance now treats hand hygiene as
the primary measure for preventing **healthcare-associated infection**, infection acquired in the
course of medical care [@who2009handhygiene].

## One Health {#sec-trans-onehealth}

**One Health** is the principle that human, animal and environmental health are interdependent, and
that infections are best understood and controlled across all three. The connections are practical:

- Most emerging infections come from animals, so surveillance in animals gives earlier warning.
- Antimicrobials used in animals select resistant bacteria that reach people through food, water and
  direct contact.
- Changes in land use, climate and travel alter where vectors can live and which animals humans meet.

Singapore offers several examples. Dengue control acts on the vector, including the release of male
mosquitoes carrying *Wolbachia* ([*The microbial world*](microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-harmless)). In
1999, Nipah virus spread from pigs imported from Malaysia to abattoir workers in Singapore: 11 fell ill
and one died [@paton1999nipah]. In 2015, an outbreak of severe group B streptococcal infection was
linked to eating raw freshwater fish, and the strain responsible also infects farmed fish
[@kalimuddin2017gbs]. Melioidosis is acquired from soil and surface water, and cases rise after heavy
rain ([*Microbes and their hosts*](host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-case)).

Controlling an outbreak depends on identifying the organism responsible and on removing it from hands,
instruments and surfaces. Both are the subject of [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](detection-control.qmd).
